terms: Acerbo Law (1923)
Electoral law granting two-thirds of seats to the party gaining at least 25% of the vote.
Corporate State
Fascist economic model organising employers and workers into state-supervised corporations.
Lateran Pacts (1929)
Agreements with the Vatican recognising Vatican City and Catholicism as the state religion.
March on Rome
Fascist demonstration of October 1922 that led to Mussolini's appointment as Prime Minister by King Victor Emmanuel III.
Matteotti Crisis (1924)
Political crisis following the murder of socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti, after which Mussolini openly imposed dictatorship.
Pact of Steel (1939)
Military alliance between Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany.
Alliances
Pre-1914 system tying powers to mutual defence: Triple Entente vs Triple Alliance.
Imperialism
Great-power competition for colonies and spheres of influence that heightened tensions.
July Crisis
Diplomatic sequence in 1914 after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand that led to general war.
Militarism
Glorification of armed forces and willingness to use them, expressed in the pre-1914 arms race.
Nationalism
Belief in the nation-state which inflamed both Great Power rivalries and Balkan separatism.
Schlieffen Plan
German strategy to defeat France quickly through Belgium before turning east against Russia.
Containment
US strategy formulated by George Kennan to limit the geographical spread of Soviet power.
Iron Curtain
Term used by Churchill in March 1946 (Fulton, Missouri) to describe the division of Europe.
Marshall Plan (1948)
US economic aid programme for European recovery worth around $13 billion.
Potsdam Conference (July-Aug 1945)
Conference of Truman, Stalin and Attlee (after replacing Churchill) finalising post-war arrangements.
Truman Doctrine (1947)
US pledge to support free peoples resisting subjugation, marking the policy of containment.
Yalta Conference (Feb 1945)
Meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin to plan the post-war world in the Crimea.
Capitulations of Santa Fe
April 1492 agreement granting Columbus titles and a share of profits from any lands discovered.
Christopher Columbus
Genoese navigator who reached the Caribbean in 1492 under the Spanish Crown.
Cipango
Marco Polo's name for Japan, Columbus's intended destination.
Reconquista
Centuries-long Iberian effort to reconquer the peninsula from Muslim rule, completed in 1492.
Taíno
Indigenous people of the Greater Antilles encountered by Columbus.
Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)
Spanish-Portuguese agreement dividing newly 'discovered' lands along a meridian west of the Cape Verde Islands.

hl-regional-option-history-of-africa-the.d: HL Regional Option: History of Africa & the Middle East
terms: Algerian War 1954-62
FLN-led struggle against France; Battle of Algiers 1956-57; ended with Evian Accords March 1962 and de Gaulle's recognition.
Ghana independence 1957
Kwame Nkrumah led Gold Coast to independence on 6 March 1957; first sub-Saharan African colony to break free from Britain.
Mau Mau Uprising 1952-60
Kikuyu-led insurgency in British Kenya; brutal counter-insurgency in detention camps; Kenyatta became President in 1964.
Organisation of African Unity 1963
Founded 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 states under Haile Selassie; promoted unity and decolonisation.
Pan-Africanism
Movement advocating African unity; fifth Pan-African Congress 1945 in Manchester featured Nkrumah, Kenyatta and Du Bois.
Year of Africa 1960
Seventeen African states gained independence in 1960 including Nigeria, Senegal, Cameroon and the Congo.

hl-regional-option-history-of-asia-ocean.d: HL Regional Option: History of Asia & Oceania
terms: Bandung Conference 1955
29 Asian and African states met April 1955 in Indonesia; Sukarno, Nehru, Nasser, Zhou Enlai promoted Non-Aligned Movement.
Indochina War 1946-54
Viet Minh under Ho Chi Minh and Giap defeated French forces at Dien Bien Phu May 1954; Geneva Accords partitioned Vietnam at 17th parallel.
Indonesian National Revolution 1945-49
Sukarno declared independence 17 August 1945; armed struggle against Dutch ended with Round Table Conference December 1949.
Malayan Emergency 1948-60
British counter-insurgency against MCP guerrillas; Briggs Plan resettlement of 500,000 Chinese into New Villages.
Philippine independence 1946
United States granted independence 4 July 1946 under Tydings-McDuffie Act timetable; Manuel Roxas first president.
Vietnam War 1955-75
Conflict between North Vietnamese DRV and US-backed South Vietnam; Tet Offensive 1968; fall of Saigon 30 April 1975.

hl-regional-option-history-of-europe.d: HL Regional Option: History of Europe
terms: Civil War 1918-21
Red Army (Bolsheviks) vs White Army plus foreign intervention; Reds won via War Communism, Cheka terror, central control.
Dual power
Coexistence of Provisional Government and Petrograd Soviet; Lenin's slogan was 'All power to the Soviets'.
February Revolution 1917
Spontaneous uprising in Petrograd (8 March NS / 23 Feb OS) caused by bread shortages; Tsar Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March.
Lenin's April Theses
April 1917 program calling for socialist revolution, end to WWI, no Provisional Government, land to peasants.
October Revolution 1917
Bolshevik seizure of power on 25 October OS / 7 November NS in Petrograd; storming of Winter Palace.
Provisional Government
Liberal-led government (March-Oct 1917) committed to continuing WWI; Prince Lvov then Kerensky led it.

hl-regional-option-history-of-the-americ.d: HL Regional Option: History of the Americas
terms: Civil rights and social movements
Post-1945 campaigns for equality included the African American civil rights movement and indigenous, feminist and youth movements across the hemisphere.
Great Depression in the Americas
The 1929 crash hit the whole hemisphere; responses included Roosevelt's New Deal in the USA and state-led economic policies across Latin America.
Independence movements
Revolutions of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries freed the Thirteen Colonies in 1776 and, under leaders like Bolivar and San Martin, much of Latin America.
Populist leaders
Leaders such as Juan Peron in Argentina built mass support through nationalism, welfare benefits and direct appeals to urban workers.
The Cold War and the Americas
US containment shaped the region through events such as the Guatemalan coup of 1954, the Cuban Revolution of 1959 and the missile crisis of 1962.
US Civil War 1861-65
Conflict between the Union and the Confederacy rooted in slavery and sectional rivalry, ending in Union victory and abolition through the 13th Amendment.
Choosing a question
A strong investigation needs a focused, debatable question on a topic at least ten years in the past, narrow enough to answer well in the word limit.
Historical investigation
A 2,200-word independent inquiry into a historical question of your choice, worth 25 marks, marked by your teacher and moderated by the IB.
Origins, purpose and content
Source evaluation must analyse value and limitations with explicit reference to each source's origins, purpose and content.
Section 1: Evaluation of sources
You identify two sources of central relevance to your question and analyse their value and limitations, for up to 6 marks.
Section 2: The investigation
The core of the task: a focused, well-evidenced argument that answers your question using a range of sources, worth up to 15 marks.
Section 3: Reflection
A discussion of what carrying out the investigation revealed to you about the methods used by, and challenges facing, historians, worth up to 4 marks.
Civil War 1918-21
Red Army (Bolsheviks) vs White Army plus foreign intervention; Reds won via War Communism, Cheka terror, central control.
Dual power
Coexistence of Provisional Government and Petrograd Soviet; Lenin's slogan was 'All power to the Soviets'.

Spontaneous uprising in Petrograd (8 March NS / 23 Feb OS) caused by bread shortages; Tsar Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March.
Lenin's April Theses
April 1917 program calling for socialist revolution, end to WWI, no Provisional Government, land to peasants.
October Revolution 1917
Bolshevik seizure of power on 25 October OS / 7 November NS in Petrograd; storming of Winter Palace.
Provisional Government
Liberal-led government (March-Oct 1917) committed to continuing WWI; Prince Lvov then Kerensky led it.

world-history-topics-two-same-as-sl.d: World History Topics (two, same as SL)
terms: Appeasement
British and French policy reaching its peak at Munich Conference September 1938 with Chamberlain's 'peace for our time' claim.
Failure of collective security
League of Nations failed to deter Japan in Manchuria 1931 and Italy in Abyssinia 1935; Hoare-Laval Pact discredited it.
Hitler's foreign policy
Lebensraum, rearmament 1935, Rhineland 1936, Anschluss 1938 and Sudetenland 1938 progressively dismantled Versailles.
Invasion of Poland September 1939
Germany invaded 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war 3 September; Soviet invasion from east 17 September.
Nazi-Soviet Pact August 1939
Ribbentrop and Molotov signed non-aggression pact with secret protocols dividing Poland and the Baltics.
Treaty of Versailles legacy
Diktat resentment, Article 231 war guilt, reparations and the loss of 13% of German territory fuelled revisionism.
Indian National Congress (INC)
Political organisation founded in 1885 that became the main vehicle of Indian nationalism.
Lahore Resolution (1940)
Muslim League resolution demanding 'independent states' for Muslims in north-western and eastern India.
Mahatma Gandhi
Indian nationalist leader whose philosophy of non-violent resistance (satyagraha) defined the freedom struggle.
Mountbatten Plan
British plan for partition leading to independence on 14-15 August 1947.
Muslim League
Party led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah which demanded a separate Muslim state.
Salt March (1930)
Gandhi's 240-mile march to Dandi to defy the British salt monopoly.
Lytton Report (1932)
League of Nations enquiry condemning Japan's actions, prompting its withdrawal from the League.
Manchukuo
Puppet state established by Japan in Manchuria in 1932 under Pu Yi.
Marco Polo Bridge Incident (July 1937)
Clash near Beijing that triggered full-scale war between Japan and China.
Mukden Incident (1931)
Staged sabotage of the South Manchurian Railway used to justify Japanese seizure of Manchuria.
Nanjing Massacre (1937-38)
Mass killings and atrocities committed by Japanese forces after the fall of Nanjing.
Tripartite Pact (1940)
Alliance between Germany, Italy and Japan formalising the Axis.
Khwarezmian campaign
Mongol invasion of the Khwarezmian Empire 1219-1221, triggered by the murder of Mongol envoys.
Kurultai
Great assembly of Mongol chiefs which proclaimed Temüjin as Genghis Khan in 1206.
Pax Mongolica
Period of relative stability across Eurasia under Mongol rule, facilitating Silk Road trade.
Temüjin
Birth name of Genghis Khan, who united the Mongol tribes by 1206.
Tumen
Mongol military unit of 10,000 cavalry, organised in a decimal system.
Yassa
Code of law promulgated by Genghis Khan to govern the Mongol empire.
Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
Supreme Court ruling declaring racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional.
Civil Rights Act (1964)
Federal law banning discrimination on the basis of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.
March on Washington (1963)
200,000-strong demonstration where Dr King delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech.
Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-56)
Year-long boycott of Montgomery's segregated buses sparked by Rosa Parks' arrest.
Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC)
Civil rights organisation founded by Martin Luther King Jr. and others in 1957.
Voting Rights Act (1965)
Federal legislation outlawing discriminatory practices preventing African Americans from voting.

prescribed-subject-military-leaders-conq.d: Prescribed Subject: Military Leaders / Conquest & its Impact / Move to Global War / Rights & Protest / Diplomatic Crises
terms: Berlin Blockade 1948-49
Stalin blocked land access to West Berlin; West responded with airlift delivering 2.3 million tons of supplies.
Long Telegram 1946
George Kennan's February 1946 cable from Moscow analysing Soviet expansionism; basis for containment policy.
Marshall Plan 1948
European Recovery Program; $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe; rejected by Stalin for Eastern bloc.
Potsdam Conference July 1945
Truman, Attlee and Stalin; disagreements over reparations and Poland; Truman hinted at atomic bomb.
Truman Doctrine 1947
March 1947 pledge to support free peoples resisting subjugation; $400 million aid to Greece and Turkey.
Yalta Conference February 1945
Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreed on UN, German occupation zones, free Polish elections; tensions over Eastern Europe.

world-history-topic-authoritarian-states.d: World History Topic: Authoritarian States (20th Century)
terms: Conditions for rise
Economic crisis, weak democratic institutions, defeat or humiliation in war and charismatic leadership common to Mussolini, Hitler, Stalin and Mao.
Economic transformation
Autarky in Italy and Germany; Five-Year Plans under Stalin; Great Leap and collectivisation under Mao.
Foreign policy
Expansionism via Abyssinia 1935, Anschluss 1938, Polish invasion 1939, Korean War involvement and Sino-Soviet split 1960.
Propaganda and culture
Goebbels' Reich Ministry, Mussolini's Minculpop, Soviet socialist realism and Maoist little red book shaped public consciousness.
Terror and surveillance
Gestapo, OVRA, NKVD and Public Security Bureau combined informers, secret police and forced-labour camps to crush opposition.
Use of ideology
Fascism (Mussolini), National Socialism (Hitler), Marxism-Leninism (Stalin), Maoism — each provided justifying doctrine and mass mobilisation.

world-history-topic-causes-effects-of-20.d: World History Topic: Causes & Effects of 20th-Century Wars
terms: Effects on civilians
Civilians suffered occupation, bombing of cities, genocide including the Holocaust, and mass displacement of refugees.
Long-term causes
Underlying economic, territorial and ideological rivalries, such as the alliance blocs and arms races that preceded the First World War.
Practices of war
Technology shaped fighting: trench warfare and artillery dominated the First World War, while blitzkrieg, strategic bombing and atomic weapons marked the Second.
Results of wars
Outcomes included peace settlements such as Versailles in 1919, new organisations like the United Nations in 1945, territorial change and social transformation.
Short-term causes
Immediate crises and triggers, such as the assassination of Franz Ferdinand in June 1914 or the German invasion of Poland in September 1939.
Total war
Twentieth-century wars mobilised whole societies and economies through conscription, rationing, propaganda and the home front.
Armed struggle
Some movements fought wars of independence, such as the FLN's campaign against French rule in Algeria from 1954 to 1962.
Challenges after independence
New states faced partition and communal violence, as in India and Pakistan in 1947, plus nation-building, economic dependence and ethnic division.
Nationalism
A sense of shared identity based on language, religion, history or territory that fuelled demands for self-rule against imperial powers.
Non-violent resistance
Methods such as Gandhi's satyagraha campaigns in India, including non-cooperation and the 1930 Salt March, put moral and political pressure on Britain.
Origins of independence movements
Opposition to imperial rule grew from economic exploitation, racial discrimination, wartime upheaval and the spread of nationalist and anti-colonial ideas.
Role of leaders
Figures such as Gandhi, Nehru, Nkrumah and Ho Chi Minh shaped strategy, built mass movements and negotiated or fought for independence.
Black Death 1347-51
Plague spread west along trade routes, killing perhaps a third or more of Europe's population and transforming wages, labour and landholding.
Feudal relationships
Across medieval Europe, land was held in exchange for service and loyalty, binding lords, vassals and peasants in a hierarchy of obligation.
Manorialism
The manor was the basic economic unit: peasants worked the lord's land and their own strips, owing labour services and dues, with serfs tied to the estate.
Religion and society
Religious institutions structured daily life: the Church dominated education and charity in Europe, while madrasas and waqf endowments served similar roles in the Islamic world.
Towns and guilds
Trade revival after about 1000 swelled towns, where merchant and craft guilds regulated quality, prices and the training of apprentices and journeymen.
Trade networks
Long-distance routes such as the Silk Roads, the Hanseatic League in northern Europe and Italian Mediterranean shipping linked Europe, the Islamic world and Asia.
Feudalism
System of political and military relationships in which lords granted land (fiefs) to vassals in return for service.
Fief
Estate granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for homage and military service.
Homage
Formal act in which a vassal pledged loyalty and service to a lord.
Manorialism
Economic system organising agricultural production around the lord's manor and peasant labour.
Serf
Unfree peasant tied to the land of a manor, owing labour and dues to a lord.
Three-field system
Crop rotation in which a third of arable land lay fallow each year, increasing productivity from c.800 onward.
General Secretary
Party post Stalin held from 1922, giving him control of personnel and the apparat.
Left Opposition
Group around Trotsky, Zinoviev and Kamenev opposing Stalin in the mid-1920s.
Lenin's Testament
Document of 1922-23 in which Lenin criticised potential successors, especially Stalin.
Permanent Revolution
Trotsky's doctrine emphasising the need to spread revolution internationally.
Right Opposition
Group around Bukharin defending NEP and gradual industrialisation.
Socialism in One Country
Stalin's slogan from 1924 prioritising the consolidation of Soviet power.
